Thanks again for the quick intro yesterday. As discussed, our security and network teams want a focused review of how Redwood's control plane will operate from within our VPC when we go private (VPC peering / Transit Gateway options). I've attached our current network diagram (acme_vpc_diagram_v3.pdf) and an access matrix we use for vendor onboarding.

High level asks:

- Any traffic flow that would traverse the public internet vs staying inside the VPC

We'd like to finalize the notes before our security review on Friday. Can you loop in the engineering owner?

Janelle

Thanks for the diagrams, Janelle. Looping in Dev (platform) and Laura (infosec).

Preliminary comments before we dig in:
- We'll send a short reference diagram (redwood_reference_controlplane_diagram.png) showing the split between control plane (managed by Redwood) and data plane (runs in ACME VPC). That will make firewall rules and routing clear.
- Control plane endpoints: control.redwood.com (API + control signals), metrics.redwood.com (pull/push depending on config), and a short list of AWS STS/Cognito endpoints for role exchange. We'll enumerate exact FQDNs/CIDRs in the follow-up.
- Connectivity modes we support: PrivateLink (recommended where available), Transit Gateway/Peering (acceptable for large networks), and IPSec VPN (fallback). PrivateLink avoids hairpinning through the public internet and simplifies ACLs — good for compliance.

Action items from us:
1) Dev will draft a port/CIDR matrix and call out any egress NAT requirements.
2) Laura will highlight audit/logging and KMS key exchange notes.
3) I'll produce the annotated diagram and circulate.

Can you confirm whether ACME prefers an AWS-native model (TGW/PrivateLink) or if there are multi-cloud connectivity constraints?

- Priyom

Thanks — quick technical notes below (will attach the access matrix as a spreadsheet):

Summary of recommended topology (AWS example):
- Data plane (in ACME VPC): Redwood inference workers run inside customer subnets (private subnets in a dedicated ASG/ASG-equivalent) with an ENI that communicates with the control plane over PrivateLink.
- Control plane (Redwood managed): REST/gRPC endpoints in our control plane VPC. Customers access control plane endpoints via PrivateLink (interface VPC endpoints).
- Routing: ensure route tables in the customer VPC point to the VPC endpoint for control plane FQDNs; no IGW egress required for control plane traffic. Public egress may still be required for OS package updates unless you use a managed bastion/NAT.

Ports/Protocols (high level):
- 443/TCP to control.redwood.com (API & control websocket upgrades)
- 443/TCP to metrics.redwood.com (TLS – push or pull depending on mode)
- 443/TCP to sts.amazonaws.com (if cross-account role exchange is used)
- Optional: 22/TCP (bastion) only if you want SSH access to data-plane hosts; we can also provide ephemeral support tunnels initiated from inside the VPC.

KMS & Secrets:
- Customer-managed CMKs for any data-at-rest encryption keys we store on behalf of ACME — recommend cross-account key policy and least-privilege roles.

HA and failover:
- Control plane endpoints are regional. We support multi-region control plane fallbacks if you want cross-region redundancy — this requires additional endpoints/PrivateLinks.

Notes on Transit Gateway vs PrivateLink:
- PrivateLink: best for strong isolation and simpler security posture. Slightly higher per-connection cost but minimal routing complexity.
- Transit Gateway: scalable for many VPCs and shared services, but traffic may traverse shared resources and requires more careful route management. Latency tradeoffs depend on topology.

I'll attach an initial port/CIDR sheet (network_access_matrix.xlsx) with suggested CIDRs for control plane egress and the minimal security group rules.

Cheers,
Dev

Hi team — a couple security points for the review doc:

- Audit/logging: we recommend forwarding VPC Flow Logs and application audit logs to ACME's central log account or to a mutually agreed S3 bucket with restricted access and retention policies. We'll include example CloudWatch/Grafana dashboards for token usage and anomalous request rates.
- Access model: prefer short-lived role assumptions (STS) and OIDC where possible; avoid long-lived static credentials in the data plane.
- Key management: if ACME requires customer-managed keys, we'll provide a KMS key policy template for cross-account decrypt only; Redwood will not be able to export the plaintext key material.
- Pen test / network scans: we'll agree a narrow maintenance window and a pre-approved scan plan; Redwood's infra team will coordinate.

Please confirm any regulatory constraints (PCI/PHI) so we can call out control plane hardening.

- Laura
From: Janelle Morris <janelle@acme-cloud.com>

Thanks all — this is exactly what we needed. Attaching an updated diagram (acme_vpc_diagram_v3.pdf was updated to include the Transit Gateway route table notes) and we've uploaded the revised network_access_matrix.xlsx into the Google Drive folder.

ACME decision: we prefer PrivateLink for the initial rollout for compliance reasons, with a TGW option for later scale. We'll expect the PrivateLink endpoint list and the exact CIDRs so our networking team can pre-provision endpoints and route tables before the kickoff on 2026-02-12.

Next steps:
- Priyom: send the annotated control plane diagram and a two-page checklist (rules, CIDRs, DNS names) by EOD tomorrow.
- Dev: finalize the access matrix and share the spreadsheet link.
- Laura: include KMS policy template and the short-lived role example in the shared Drive.
- Marissa: I'll coordinate procurement redlines and share the PO template.

Appreciate the quick turnaround. Looking forward to the kickoff.

Best,
Janelle
